newsitem.title: BELARUS: Opposition to Belarus's Lukashenko hesitates.
newsitem.headline: Opposition to Belarus's Lukashenko hesitates.

text.p: International concern grew at the political crisis in Belarus on Tuesday, but President Alexander Lukashenko's parliamentary opponents seemed at a loss over how to stop him going ahead with a much-criticised referendum.
Weary deputies, who have been occupying parliament around the clock since Friday, debated their next moves for hours on Tuesday morning -- and decided to break until 4 p.m. (1400 GMT).
Deputy speaker Gennady Karpenko said the world was closely watching the conflict in the former Soviet republic of 10 million sparked by Lukashenko's bid to increase his powers.
"We are not an isolated country and we do not want to become one. We do not want to build a new Berlin Wall around us," he said. Pro-Russian Lukashenko has shown indifference to outside criticism.
The United States and other governments expressed concern at events in the country sandwiched between Russia and Poland.
Eastern neighbour Russia, linked with Belarus in a much-vaunted two-state "community", called on Tuesday for compromise and common sense in Belarus.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said President Boris Yeltsin had discussed Belarus at a 90-minute meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

"The president and the prime minister expressed alarm about rising tension in Belarus society and the hope that common sense and the art of political compromise will replace the ambitions and confrontations among politicians," he said.
Neighbouring Ukraine's parliament also expressed concern on Tuesday but its mildly-worded resolution avoided taking sides.

The most outspoken criticism of Lukashenko has come from leading German parliamentarian Karsten Voigt, president of the North Atlantic Assembly, who said Lukashenko's behaviour was "illegal, non-democratic and sometimes even crazy".

Lukashenko, defying a spate of rulings by the constitutional court and parliament saying Sunday's referendum should carry no legal force, is seeking authority to extend his term by more than two years and widen his powers over all institutions.

More than 80 deputies on Monday signed a request to the constitutional court to start impeachment proceedings against Lukashenko, but it appeared certain the president, who controls the security forces and all the real levers of executive authority, would take no notice.
A spokesman told Reuters the court was preparing to consider the proposal but no ruling would be made on Tuesday.
Lukashenko's closest aide, Vladimir Zametalin, said the president had "many options" and hinted that he could dissolve parliament and court if they impeached him.
Prime Minister Mikhail Chigir resigned on Monday when Lukashenko refused to drop the referendum, giving the opposition a boost, but Lukashenko quickly replaced him.
The 42-year-old president, in a late-night television interview, said he had accepted Chigir's resignation and had made deputy prime minister Sergei Ling acting prime minister.

On Monday government spokesman Dmitry Malinovsky said Ling had taken over Chigir's duties though the former premier was still clearing his office. Chigir has yet to speak publicly about his decision to quit.

A pro-Lukashenko deputy, Ivan Pashkevich, told Reuters Lukashenko did not want confrontation and would meet parliamentary leaders and the cabinet on returning from Borisov, about 100 km (65 miles) east of Minsk where he was continuing his pre-referendum campaign. There was no confirmation.
Lacking a quorum on Tuesday, exhausted parliamentarians seemed unsure about their next move. Some pushed for action anyway, but others argued to continue their tactic of sticking to the constitution.

Lukashenko, at a rally on Monday in Gomel, appeared in no mood to compromise. He told political opponents who accuse him of dictatorial ambitions to be ready to flee Belarus if he wins the referendum on November 24.
